### Graph random seed inheritance on save and in nested graphs

Saving a graph that omitted its random seed used to write an absolute zero. When another graph called that file, the reference renderer restarted its random stream at zero. MaterialCraft also ignored a child's authored seed mode when cooking an instance. The SBS reader, writer and evaluator now preserve how the child obtains its seed. An absolute seed starts a new stream. Either relative mode adds the child's signed offset to the resolved instance seed, wrapping at 32 bits. The graph properties panel and the `graph.seed` command expose inheritance. Grouping nodes keeps the original standalone seed and offsets it at the new instance so later parent seed edits still reach the grouped nodes.

Build a child containing a single grayscale F32 Pixel Processor that returns Random(1). Connect an instance of that child to the parent output. Use child seeds omitted, absolute 0 or 5, parent-relative 0 or 5, and input-relative 5. For each, use an omitted instance seed, absolute 7 and parent-relative 3. Repeat four configurations with the child in a separate SBS file. Render each at 16² with parent seeds 0 and 19 and at 32 × 16 with seed 42. Compare every F32 bit with the one-worker Direct3D 11 reference. As an independent control, render the same random field at the calculated seed with no intervening seed offset.

### Bounded work for terminal Quadrant siblings

The shared FX-Map evaluator now charges a group of at most four terminal Quadrant siblings for its first discarded stamp. Each child evaluates its own properties, applies its variable writes and reaches its own sample-grid test before it can share that charge. Each visible stamp still costs a visit. An iteration or a branch with descendants cannot obtain extra visits by repeating a single discarded stamp. Terminal nodes also skip the unused child-center and child-seed calculations.

The ordinary limit covers 1,048,576 visits plus the same number of individual discards. Every group with an extra discard needs a distinct parent and first discarded child among those ordinary visits. At most three further discards can share their charge, bounding evaluated visits at 5,242,880. Stored stamps, stack occupancy, raster copies and pixel work retain their own bounds. A regression with a 64-visit allowance checks a visible marker and 48 four-child groups that miss all 4×4 samples. Changing those children to visible squares reaches the limit. Repeating a branch with a single missed child 80 times also reaches it. The previous cook failed on the marker case.

### Scalar float precision in nested graph instances

A scalar float supplied by an instance default, an explicit constant or a constant expression retains literal precision inside the child graph. A value driven by an exposed parent parameter retains runtime precision. In an original Pixel Processor, take the sine of one full turn using the F32 constant 6.2831855. The fixed result has F32 bits `343bbd2e`. With the same turn supplied by an exposed parent input it has bits `80000000`. A called function writing a different variable preserves this distinction. MaterialCraft now tracks fixed scalar floats at graph boundaries and invalidates known operands by the names a called function writes.

Use the signed procedural RGBA fields from the [pixel interpolation comparison](#packed-products-in-the-second-endpoint-of-a-pixel-interpolation). Use field indices 0, 1, 2, 0, 0 and 1 with seeds 435071 + 19j for j from 0 through 5. Read the red channel with nearest sampling. Set the exposed turns to 1, .1875, −.38157, .723561, 0 and .375. Compare top-level reads, literal 1 and .375, nested defaults, explicit values, a .375 + .625 expression, a parent read and a parent-driven selection between 1 and .375. ### Rectangular image inputs on graph instances

When a connected image crosses a graph boundary, axes more than one doubling or halving from their target move first. The final sampling pass adjusts both axes to the requested dimensions. Each pass stores its result at the input bridge's precision. A 32² F32 image feeding a 16 × 8 F16 bridge therefore goes through 32 × 16. MaterialCraft previously used 16² as the intermediate. The connected bridge now shares the atomic input filters' choice of intermediate dimensions.

Connect a parent color input to a child color input fixed at 16 × 8. Wire the child input directly to its output. At size index j, use parent dimensions (16,8), (16,16), (32,16), (32,32), (64,64), (128,32), (64,16), (4,4), (8,2), (32,4), (128,2), (8,64), (4,1), (2,2) and (128,128), in that order. Set seed s = 430031 + 37j. For channel c and width w, compute the unsigned 32-bit word q = (x + wy + s + 701c) × 1597334677 + 3812015801, then q = (q XOR (q >> 16)) × 2246822519, wrapping both products. Generate F32 sign bit (q >> 15) & 1, biased exponent 120 + q mod 10, and fraction (q >> 1) & 0x7fffff. Compare all four stored channels at every output pixel.

| Parent → child storage | Settings | Previous exact / total · max | Corrected exact / total · max |

| F32 → F16 | 15 | 913/1,920 · .00390625 | 1,920/1,920 · 0 |
| F16 → F16 | 15 | 904/1,920 · .00390625 | 1,920/1,920 · 0 |
| F32 → F32 | 15 | 929/1,920 · 4.76837158e−7 | 1,920/1,920 · 0 |
| U16 → F32 | 15 | 969/1,920 · 1.15036964e−5 | 1,920/1,920 · 0 |
| F16 → U8 | 15 | 1,046/1,920 · 191 levels | 1,920/1,920 · 0 |

### Copied steps in called pixel sums

The shared pixel evaluator now follows a floating-point product copied to another variable. A later addition can use its original factors after the first variable is overwritten. Reading a component of the copy separately rounds that component. The same behavior applies when the next addition or the component read is in the caller or a subsequent function call.

Use the four F32 settings from the [component and assignment-order comparison](#component-reads-and-writes-across-pixel-function-calls). Inside the call, copy the step to another variable, overwrite the original with the position, and add the captured step to the position. Compare a single unused copy, a second unused copy, an explicit read of the copy, and a read in a later call. In three further graphs, append the saved B component after the first three sum components, reading B inside the call or in the caller. As a control, overwrite the copy with the position before reading it.

### Switch Blend with parameter-driven endpoint opacity

An unmasked Switch Blend with opacity 0 or 1 can forward the selected floating-point color texture when opacity is fixed and storage precision matches. When its opacity reads an exposed graph parameter, the color conversion runs even at matching precision. ### Signed zero when Switch Blend selects a floating-point color input

In the [first eighth specular pass](#environment-and-intermediate-precision-in-the-eighth-specular-passes), render the black-specular-and-roughness control at 128² with F32 storage on the first pixel processor. Their formats are F32, F16 and F16. The first Switch matched 16,345/16,384 and the second 16,353/16,384. Maximum numerical error was zero at all five stages. At (1,22) the first Switch returned `80000000` on green in MaterialCraft and `00000000` in the reference.

An unmasked Switch at opacity zero or one copies the selected input. A same-size floating-point RGBA copy at the same precision preserves every channel bit. When converting F16 to F32 or F32 to F16, an existing zero retains its sign only when all three source RGB signs are negative. This also governs an existing zero in alpha. Converting before rounding to F16 preserves the sign of a negative nonzero component that rounds to zero. Subnormal F32 channels become signed zero before this precision conversion. At fractional weights the foreground and background channels, the rounded foreground product and the resulting multiply-add each flush subnormals to signed zero.

Feed two nearest-sampling pixel processors into an unmasked Switch. For component c of each F32 RGBA field select words from `00000000 80000000 b1800000 31800000 bf800000 3f800000 3e8b217c bfd382af 80000001 00000001 c0000000 3b0386a1 b8899021 38f061d5 bf6987c4 405ccaac`. Use F32 for both processors at opacities 0, 1, .25 and .6137. Repeat with an F16 foreground at 0, 1, .5 and .6137. Store the Switch in all four formats at the first size and in F32 at the other two.

For independent sign tests, use 16², 32 × 16 and 16 × 32. For source s = 0 for foreground or 1 for background, take bit c of (x + 5y + 7j + 3s) modulo 16 as the sign. Store all four formats at the first size and F16 and F32 at the others. The sixteen sign masks distinguish the three RGB signs from all four channel signs, the first two signs and unconditional zero clearing.

For a separate field around the smallest normal F32 value, use 16 × 32, 32 × 16 and 32² at seeds 404127 + 19j. Use the same eight graphs as the first comparison. Use index (7x + y + 5c + 7j) modulo 16 for foreground or (3x + 5y + 3c + 7j + 1) modulo 16 for background. Store all four formats at the first size and both floating formats at the others. ### Stored products in pixel expressions and irradiance ray steps

A straight-line pixel expression can assign a vector product to a variable and add it to several positions. For each component consumed only by additions, the evaluator now rounds the multiply and add together. The change applies to the shared expression evaluator.

Use the original signed RGBA32F fields and seven settings from the [packed interpolation comparison](#packed-products-in-the-second-endpoint-of-a-pixel-interpolation). Replace q with ((q XOR (q >> 16)) × 2246822519) modulo 2³². Use bit 13 for the sign, 123 + (q modulo 5) for the biased exponent, and bits 1 through 23 for the fraction. Use seed 394167 + 23j. ### Packed products in the second endpoint of a pixel interpolation

At 64² in the [world-position plane light](#panoramic-line-light-and-horizon-across-the-seam), separately returning the two endpoints and scalar weight from the final interpolation gave 4,096/4,096 exact F32 pixels at each readout. The interpolated output matched 4,084/4,096. Its second endpoint packs RGB multiplied by exposure alongside a constant alpha. At (21,3), rounding the blue product before subtracting the first endpoint gives output bits `3ebaed06`. Combining that product with the subtraction gives the measured `3ebaed07`. This calculation reproduced all 4,096 pixels. The shared pixel evaluator now carries the factors of each eligible component through packing into the interpolation. A separate read of a product lane preserves its rounded value. If the interpolation and a subsequent add both consume the product, each can fuse it with its own addend.

For the independent graphs, sample one original RGBA32F field at texel centers. For (width,height) = (64,32), (32,64), (64,64), number the fields j from zero. For channel c from zero let q be ((x + width × y) × (747796405 + 2c) + 2891336453 + 19998479c + 78571j) modulo 2³². Use bit 13 of q for the sign, 125 + ((q >> 25) modulo 3) for the biased F32 exponent, and bits 1 through 23 for the fraction. Use seed 379131 + 41j. Run F32 at all sizes, add U8, U16 and F16 at 64 × 32, then repeat its F32 setting.

Use first endpoint (B,R,A,G), second endpoint (R×A,G×A,B×A,.625) and weight G. Test this graph, reversed endpoints, and identical packed endpoints. Also test returning the independently rounded blue product alongside the mixed RGB, adding the second endpoint to the mix, selecting lanes YWZX from the second endpoint, dividing RGB by A, using RGBA×A directly, and packing (R×A,G×A,R×B,B×G). At (11,0), the second-endpoint case gives RGB bits `bd551682 bef1e18c bec17c27`. Returning the blue product changes just the mixed blue to `bec17c28`. The separate product reads `3f1cb4a3`.

### Reciprocal division through pixel function calls

The two eighth specular passes divide a lighting term by the Z component of a normalized direction. Returning the environment lookup alone matched the 128-pixel scanline through (62,57) of the second pass. Returning the scalar lighting quotient exposed a rounding difference. Both operands matched at that pixel. In a separate original graph, the pixel expression `A / (1 / B)` reproduced A × B throughout the signed field. At (1,0) the inputs have F32 words `40763400` and `3f68c2ba`. A separate read of the inner reciprocal returns `3f8cc7a2`. The outer quotient returns `405fda66`. Supplying the one from a sampled channel returns `405fda65`. The latter control matched before the change.

The pixel evaluator now retains the original factor through scalar calls, vector construction, component selection and multiplication by a literal unit lane. Other readers of the reciprocal receive its rounded value. A sole downstream add or subtract can contract with the resulting product. The original operands still evaluate in graph order. The two measured roots use their existing SBS operations. Loop-carried reciprocal factors remain unmeasured.

Use a nearest-filtered four-channel F32 procedural input. Number pixels in row-major order from zero and number the fields j = 0, 1, 2. Use sizes 64 × 32, 32 × 64 and 64², with seeds 364801 + 31j. Let m be the low 32 bits of 747796405i + 2891336453 + 997j. Red is ((1103515245i + 53719 + 57j) mod 65521)/8192 − 4. For green, combine the low 23 bits of m with exponent field 126 + ((m >> 22) mod 3). In field two use 1 + (m mod 131071)/16777216 instead. Blue is (((m >> 8) mod 257) − 128)/512. Alpha is one. At the first size, render in F32, U8, U16 and F16. Render the other sizes in F32 and return to the original F32 setting.

For the direct graphs, pack the quotient, its denominator, the underlying factor and red into RGBA. Compare ordinary division with a unit reciprocal, a connected Dot inside the expression, multiplication by one or two, a sampled numerator of one, a squared or square-root divisor, two equivalent vector-pack controls, normalization with Z equal to one or one plus blue, a reciprocal numerator of .625, and the sum of two quotients. For the call graphs, move the inverse, the division or both into reusable functions. Normalize (blue, green, Z) in a function and pass its Z lane to a scalar division function. Compare literal Z against sampled alpha. Also add two called quotients, add or subtract blue, and expose an additional read of the quotient in the sum graph. At 64 × 32 the sole-read sum matched all 2,048 fused results. The shared sum matched all 2,048 separately rounded results. For the two called quotients, contracting the left product matched all 2,048 pixels.

### Scalar Quadrant luminosity in saved packages

A Quadrant accepts a scalar luminosity in MaterialCraft. Saving that value as a one-component literal swatch produced an SBS that the reference renderer could not compile. The native swatch takes four components. A single constant scalar function is also a valid property representation, and retains the scalar’s meaning in both grayscale and color. The writer now uses that representation for a scalar literal on a Quadrant. Existing four-component swatches and authored functions retain their representations. [Writer and regression](../crates/formats/src/sbs/pattern_graph.rs)

Use one additive square covering the canvas with pattern size (4,4), zero roughness, opacity multiplier one and tiling off. Use black for the grayscale background and (.125,.25,.5,.375) for the color background. For each color mode and each luminosity in (.375,−.3125,1.5,0,1), compare three graphs. The first holds the scalar directly in MaterialCraft. The second uses a function with that scalar as its only constant. The third uses the literal swatch (.1875,.5,.8125,luminosity). Save each with the ordinary file command and reopen it. The earlier writer’s ten scalar saves were all rejected by the reference compiler. All ten corrected scalar saves, ten constant-function saves and ten swatch saves compiled.

### Position, depth and iteration in pattern expressions

Iterate supplies the zero-based repetition number. Quadrant subdivision supplies the branch position, depth and extent. Expressions on descendants can read those values. A Switch or Iterate at the root read the starting position (.5,.5). After Quadrant slots 1 and 2, each read (.625,.375). An Iterate’s initial branch keeps the enclosing number and its repeated branch starts a new counter. [Nested counter measurements](#initial-branch-of-a-nested-pattern-iterator)

### Four-child pattern order as a tile-copy batch fills

In one eight-level additive quadrant tree, each of the 16,384 depth-seven parents draws itself and four leaves. A depth-three subtree contains 256 of these parents and 1,280 logical draws. A stamp crossing the tiling window can contribute several copies. The render order changes when subtrees 58 and 59 followed by 0 and 1 reach 5,460 physical copies. In the measured continuation, subtree 2 moves later and the next prefix starts in subtree 3. The prefix starting in subtree 40 can also fill one subtree earlier. MaterialCraft counts copies in the common render and tiling window and uses the observed order within its measured range. [Four-child ordering and threshold regression](../crates/nodes/src/pattern/tile_runs/four_children.rs)

To reproduce the threshold, use a white F32 image and active additive squares. At each parent, reserve the parent and its first leaf for signed markers. Number the other three leaves in recursive slot order. For a subtree with q additional copies, place leaves with ordinal floor(768j/q) on the X seam for j from 0 through q−1. Keep the other leaves inside the unit square. In groups 58, 59, 0, 1 distribute 339 extra copies as (84,85,85,85). Do the same for groups 40 through 43 and use (84,85) for groups 2 and 3. With all other extra counts at zero, groups (58,59,0,1), (40,41,42,43) and (0,1,2,3) each account for 5,459 copies. Move one more leaf of group 58 to the seam to reach 5,460 in the first total. Two signed square markers sharing a pixel with gains −1 and 2⁻²⁵ reveal their order. Swap the gains and repeat. Seven marker pairs in the regression reverse order and two preserve it. Adding one copy to group 40 or group 2 alone preserves the earlier ordering for these pairs. The regression failed before the change.

For an independent order readout, give selected parents horizontal strips and their first leaves vertical strips. Read their F32 intersections, exchange the two gains and resolve tied ranks with individual point pairs. Refine each interval where adjacent sampled parents separate in rank. The observed order spans 35 runs before the first total fills and 33 afterwards. A separate profile with 5,461 copies in the prefix starting at group 40 locates its first cut in group 43. For the profile with 5,461 in groups 58, 59, 0 and 1, the parent ordering agreed at all 16,384 positions. Eleven of 192 nearby stamp pairs gave different orders between two dense point fields. Each of those eleven pairs was then isolated at a separate pixel, one pair per field. With seeds 335509 and 335527 and both gain assignments, all 44 isolated readouts reproduced the 33-run order.

In a second regression, use all four terminal leaf slots in the expanded-window square construction. At the 1,024 Morton-ordered readout positions the following half-open parent ranges return 2⁻²⁵. All other positions return zero. [Square construction](#eight-level-two-child-drawing-across-equal-tile-and-render-windows) · [End-to-end regression](../crates/nodes/src/pattern/tests.rs)

### Eight-level two-child drawing across equal tile and render windows

A complete eight-level additive pattern can draw a parent followed by two leaves at each of its 16,384 terminal branches. The measured single-processor pixels agree with MaterialCraft's batch size of 5,460 physical tile copies when the render and tiling windows extend beyond the unit square. MaterialCraft now counts each stamp using the actual common window when both axes wrap. This changes how overlapping F32 contributions accumulate. The measured path requires a single emitted tree and the existing checks on shape, opacity, subdivisions and batch boundaries. [Two-child batch construction](../crates/nodes/src/pattern/tile_runs/two_children.rs)

For the regression, start with a white grayscale F32 field. Place additive squares on all depth-seven parents and on their two leaves in slots 0 and 2. Superimpose the parent squares from second-level groups 0 and 5, assigning gains 2⁻²⁵ and −1 respectively. Keep all remaining draws active at gain .25. Use seed 158729, leaf width and height .875 in local coordinates, and leaf Y offset .5. Number the parents in a 32² readout in recursive child order. For each texel, interleave its five column and row bits, starting with the low column bit. [Regression geometry and readout](../crates/nodes/src/pattern/tests.rs)

| Render and tiling windows (X then Y) | Output | Readout origin | Leaf X offset | Parents returning 2⁻²⁵ | Parents returning zero |
|---|---|---|---:|---:|---:|
| (−.5,1.5), (−.5,1.5) | 256² | (64,64) | 0 | 284 | 740 |
| (0,1), (−.5,1.5) | 128 × 256 | (0,64) | −1/512 | 274 | 750 |
| (0,1), (−.5,1.5) | 128 × 256 | (0,64) | .4995 | 252 | 772 |

Each readout has one transition. The earlier renderer fails the first expanded-window readout at (0,0) relative to its origin.

For an independent comparison, number the 64 depth-three subtrees in recursive slot order. Pair the first with the last, the second with the penultimate and so on. Hold the first subtree fixed and rotate the other 63 one position to the right each round. Place pair j in cell (j mod 8, floor(j/8)) of an eight-column grid within the unit window. Both parent streams draw at that cell, with gains −1 and 2⁻²⁵. Use leaf gain .25 and frame offset (0,.5). Reverse the two parent gains for the second polarity. For size index j = 0…3 use 256², 128 × 64, 64 × 128 and 128² and rounds 0, 17, 41 and 61. Use seed 322817 + 53j + polarity. Request F32 at all sizes and U8, U16 and F16 at 128 × 64. ### Tile-copy batches across repeated six-level quadrant trees

Several six-level trees can contribute to the same pixel in a grayscale pattern. With all 1,024 depth-five parents and their four terminal children drawing, each first-level quadrant submits 1,280 stamps per tree. The four quadrants keep separate batches across repetitions. Within each tree, full batches of 5,460 physical tile copies are submitted in slot order 3, 0, 1, 2. At the end, partial batches composite in order 3, 2, 1, 0. A repeated tile can fill a batch before its other copy draws. MaterialCraft now records these boundaries before discarding stamps that miss the sample grid. The measured path covers complete trees of nonzero additive squares or analytic shape 8, with one outer repetition controller and center culling disabled. [Single-tree controls](#six-level-quadrant-draw-order-after-an-iteration-or-switch) · [Repeated-tree regression](../crates/nodes/src/pattern/tests/repeated_quadrants.rs)

Build an original white F32 graph with roughness zero. Repeat a complete quadtree, with a square on every depth-five parent and depth-six leaf. Place neutral stamps at (.875,.90625) with gain .25. Center two marked squares on the same readout texel, each .875 readout pixels wide and high. Draw −1 first and the texel retains 2⁻²⁵. Draw 2⁻²⁵ first and the addition rounds back to white before the subtraction leaves zero. Repeat each marked pair with the gains exchanged. Keep unrelated stamps active. The Rust regression on the earlier cook returned 2⁻²⁵ at (0,0) for two trees where the measured order gives zero.

With tiling off, enumerate a tree first by child slot and then recursively in child order, drawing each parent immediately before its four leaves. Pairwise strip crossings identified contiguous runs for one, two, three, four, five, eight and nine trees. With two and four trees, overlapping point markers independently confirmed all 10,239 and 20,479 neighboring stamp pairs in those runs. Each pair was read with both gain assignments. Five trees put 5,460 copies from each quadrant into its first batch. Nine trees fill two batches per quadrant. Thirteen trees gave the predicted result in all 302 additional marker pairs, including boundaries in a third full batch.

To reproduce the output comparisons, number each leaf within its first-level slot from 0 to 1,023 in recursive child order. Use two, five or nine trees. Mark leaf 0 of slot 0 in the first tree against leaf 0 of slot 3 in the second. Mark leaves 0, 1, 63, 270, 271, 272, 273, 511, 888 and 1,023 in slot 0 of the last tree against the same leaves in slot 1 of the first. Finally compare leaves 0, 275, 300 and 900 of slots 2 and 3 in the last tree. Scan the pairs in that order and take the first set that shares no stamps. For pair j put both marks at normalized position ((8 + j mod 85 + .5)/128, (12 + floor(j/85) + .5)/128), with size .875/128. Exchange the gains for the second field. Request 128², 128 × 64, 64 × 128 and 256², using seed 319463 + 17 × tree count + 31 × size index + polarity (indices start at zero). Request F32 at each size and U8, U16 and F16 at 128 × 64. Reopen every third setting in both applications, starting with the first, in size, polarity and U8/U16/F16/F32 order.

### Compositing a single seven-level tree through pattern controls

### Six-level quadrant draw order after an iteration or switch

A single grayscale quadrant tree with six levels of subdivision draws the initial quadrant and then composites its four child streams in reverse slot order. Outer iterations can still be waiting on the evaluation stack while the only active tree runs. The renderer now records where the four children start relative to those waiting iterations. A second active tree invalidates these ranges. Parameter evaluation, seed inheritance and the order inside each child stream follow the original traversal. [Direct six-level probes](#draw-order-at-six-quadrant-subdivisions)

### Three active quadrant levels in Dirt 5 and Dirt Gradient

Dirt 5 and Dirt Gradient draw a parent at depth 7, its four children and their sixteen children. In a complete tree this gives 344,064 draws before tiling. Changing the addition order changes some F32 pixels even when all three levels draw the same shape. The clean-room renderer now counts physical tile copies when splitting these runs. The order was measured with original square graphs and checked on the two root generators.

Start with a unit render and tiling region, zero roughness (the stored `hurst` parameter), a white background and a full four-child tree. Leave depths 0–6 empty. At depth 7 draw two squares at the same center with weights −1 and 2⁻²⁵. The two possible F32 results distinguish the draw order. Keep the deeper levels active and move their .25-weight squares away from the readout. Use a square width of .875 in both axes. On one reference processor, pair the 64 depth-three subtrees in 63 rounds so that each pair meets once. Reading the 256 corresponding parent centers in Morton order gives 516,096/516,096 matching comparisons. Shift the compared centers within the subtrees and test both polarities. All 818,406 eligible overlap reads across 684 frames agree with the reconstructed order. Split the 256 parent positions at 0, 4, 28, 64, 96, 128, 140, 164, 192 and 256, then bisect each interval. Comparing the midpoints of the 153 interval pairs in every subtree and both polarities gives another 19,584/19,584 exact reads. All three maxima are zero. These observations place the parents in 46 contiguous runs.

To reproduce the tile-edge regression, divide the tree into 16 depth-two subtrees, subtract each subtree origin from its depth-seven branch offset and use 128² F32 at seed 188119. Set the frames of groups 9 and 11 to zero and their weights to −1 and 2⁻²⁵ respectively. Offset all other parent frames by (.5, 0) with weight .25. Offset the children by (0, .5) and the grandchildren by (−.5/512, .5). Read the top-left 32² pixels in Morton order. The tiny positive result occurs at parent indices [796, 932) with tiling off and [784, 919) with horizontal tiling. With vertical tiling and grandchild offset (.5, −.5/512), it occurs at [784, 922). All other readout pixels are zero. Moving a grandchild over a seam changes the order of the overlapping interior parents.

For wider coverage, use shape selectors 2, 3, 4 and 6 with tiling off, horizontal, vertical and both. Keep child and grandchild base frame offsets at (0, .5). Apply the following eight changes, with seed 188119 + 37j for zero-based row j. The deltas are in unit coordinates.

| Negative, positive group | Size | Width | Child frame delta | Grandchild frame delta |
|---|---|---:|---|---|
| 12, 0 | 128² | .875 | 0 | 0 |
| 0, 14 | 128² | .875 | 0 | (−.5/512, 0) |
| 4, 13 | 128 × 64 | .875 | (.5/256, 0) | 0 |
| 10, 3 | 64 × 128 | .875 | 0 | (0, −.5/512) |
| 9, 15 | 256 × 128 | .75 | 0 | (−.5/512, 0) |
| 5, 11 | 128 × 256 | .9375 | 0 | (−.5/512, 0) |
| 12, 0 | 128² | .875 | 0 | (−.5/512, 0) |
| 12, 0 | 128² | .875 | 0 | (0, −.5/512) |

The 128 full F32 frames matched 2,359,296/2,359,296 pixels. In the square graph repeat all four tiling modes with group pairs (9,11), (7,9), (5,11) and (5,7), moving the grandchild just over each seam in turn as in the regression. These 32 frames matched 524,288/524,288. Save and reopen rows 0, 3 and 6 for horizontal squares, both-axis shape 3 and untiled shape 6. Repeat with square edge settings 0, 3 and 6 under vertical tiling, visiting X then Y for each pair in the given order. Both applications preserved their originals and agreed on all 172,032/172,032 pixels across these 12 reopens. All maxima are zero.

Test the copy threshold independently with square size .875, horizontal tiling and 128² F32. Leave the parent pairs overlapped. Each depth-three subtree has 5,376 draws. Move 0, 40, 80 or 83 grandchild squares to cross the left edge, dividing the extra copies equally among the four depth-four children and assigning remainders to the first children in Morton order. ### Paired subtree capacity in horizontally tiled Dirt Gradient

In the complete three-level generator, one early subtree can fill a batch while nearby interior squares still follow the measured order. The earlier implementation fell back as soon as any depth-three subtree reached 5,460 physical copies. The renderer now checks each pair of depth-three subtrees in the final quadrant against two batches. It also checks that every computed split lies strictly inside its measured depth-four subtree. Independent overlaps show that filling certain pairs changes the order of unrelated draws. ### Individual tile copies after two full horizontal batches

In a complete quadrant tree with four children and four grandchildren below depth seven, the horizontal generator can fill two batches in depth-three groups 58–59 or 62–63. Number groups in child-slot order. Each batch holds 5,460 physical copies. At 256² and seed zero, group pair 58–59 contributes one further copy. At 128 × 64 and seed 142327 it contributes 17. In group pair 62–63 at 128 × 64 and seed 186722, the remaining ten copies enter the batch containing group 48. The last seven copies from group 48 resume after the 15,766th depth-seven parent. Each cut can fall between the two horizontal copies of a single square.

For the three settings, give each depth-seven parent an individually addressable square and pair squares at distinct readout pixels. In the 186722 setting the seven-copy continuation falls between parent markers 90,027 and 267,456 when stamps are numbered in depth-first order starting at zero.

Each subtree receives the quotient, with one extra where (subtree + g) mod 4 is less than the remainder. Use the first stamps in each subtree's traversal order for its extra copies. For each overlapping pair the test checks whether the negative or positive square drew first. The earlier renderer returned zero on its first marker, where the reference reads 2⁻²⁵. ### Completing short paired quadrant batches in Moisture Noise

Start with the [sparse quadrant tree](#sparse-quadrant-parents-and-leaves-in-moisture-noise). A run of fewer than 5,460 submitted copies from groups 24–31 borrows the missing copies from group 52. Groups 40–47 borrow from group 56. When the paired prefix starting at 16 or 32 splits in its seventh group, its short block finishes immediately after that prefix. Other pending blocks finish after the prefix starting at 0. If that prefix splits in its seventh group, block 24 finishes first. Otherwise block 40 finishes first. The measured rule covers sixth- and seventh-group splits and borrowing strictly within the first partner group.

For the regression, enable all 16 depth-two parents and all 64 depth-three groups. In each depth-four subtree set the first q cells of the 16² depth-eight grid to .25 and the rest to zero. For the six consecutive blocks starting at groups 0, 16, 32, 8, 24 and 40, respectively, use q = (95,66,95,96,84,83), (95,95,66,84,83,82) or (66,95,95,85,82,84), and use 96 elsewhere. Draw two coincident depth-seven squares on white with gains −1 and 2⁻²⁵, then swap the gains. Compare 48 pairs per profile, including groups 24, 40, 52 and 56 against each other and the three paired prefixes. All 288 signed marker values and all 98,304 pixels in the six 128² F32 images match. The previous range calculation declined all three profiles. An independently reconstructed ordering also matches all 32,766 signed adjacent comparisons on the isolated generator's fifth setting with tiling disabled.

For the broader sweep, use PCG64 seed 205173. Enumerate sixth- and seventh-group splits independently for the three paired prefixes. ### Weighted color accumulation in the palette iteration

The K-means iteration root matches all 135,168 RGBA pixels in 33 distinct whole-root settings on one and eight processors. All ten MaterialCraft saves reopen to their original 40,960 pixels in both applications and agree across applications. The output palette is 256 × 16 at every input size. Maximum channel error is zero for every measured format.

| Root and comparison | U8 exact / total · max | U16 exact / total · max | F16 exact / total · max | F32 exact / total · max |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| One or eight processors | 16,384/16,384 · 0 | 32,768/32,768 · 0 | 20,480/20,480 · 0 | 65,536/65,536 · 0 |
| Saved packages, one processor | 4,096/4,096 · 0 | 12,288/12,288 · 0 | 4,096/4,096 · 0 | 20,480/20,480 · 0 |

The first difference was in the weighted RGB sum over each 256-sample row. The two input images and the 256² classification map already agreed bit for bit. The function multiplies each RGB component by its weight, packs the three products with a fourth weight component, then adds that vector to the running total. Preserving the product through packing allows a single F32 rounding per RGB addition. The evaluator uses these factors within the current iteration when each factor survives until the sum. A nested loop that clears a factor uses the previously stored vector value. The fourth component follows ordinary F32 addition.

| Stage | 32² input before | 64² input before | 32² input after | 64² input after |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Weighted rows | 65,416/65,536 · 3.81469727e−5 | 65,404/65,536 · 1.52587891e−5 | 65,536/65,536 · 0 | 65,536/65,536 · 0 |
| Final palette | 4,080/4,096 · 5.96046448e−8 | 4,080/4,096 · 8.94069672e−8 | 4,096/4,096 · 0 | 4,096/4,096 · 0 |

### Hue and chroma rounding near equal RGB channels

The reference retains a hue difference at equal-channel grays immediately below powers of two when saturation is raised. At hue .5, saturation 1 and lightness .5, render five 256² F32 ramps. For pixel index i from zero to 65,535, subtract i + 1 from the positive F32 bit pattern for .125, .25, .5, .75 or 1, use that value for all RGB channels and set alpha to 1. Use seeds 243109 through 243113. Below .25, .5 and 1 the last visible differences occur 49,151, 24,575 and 12,287 representable values from the center. Each is one representable step inside a distance of 3/4096. The .125 ramp reaches its final odd offset, while the .75 ramp has no visible hue difference.

At each pixel, choose the first minimum channel in R, G, B order. For a red, green or blue minimum use the channel pair (B,G), (R,B) or (G,R) and a sector of 3, 5 or 1 respectively. Adding 3/4096 to the second channel before subtraction reproduces the measured boundary. Divide that difference by chroma + 1/4096 with the pixel reciprocal, add the sector, convert sixths to turns and apply the slider displacement. For adjusted lightness L the available chroma range is 1 − |2L − 1|. Computing half that range before the multiply-add with saturation preserves the measured endpoints of dark colors. The .125 ramp now matches all 65,536 pixels.

## 2026-11-21 root comparisons

### Connected quadrant depth and amplified spot patterns

In the two BNW Spots 1 generators, disabling a deep branch changed the brightness of the root square. On the first root at 32², scale 2, roughness .6, disorder .37 and seed 113, the ratio between the original implementation and the reference matched the difference between ten and eleven octave weights. Counting connected quadrant subdivisions through switches and iterators fixed the brightness. The traversal still uses the visited drawing depth to order stamps.

An original F32 control draws one white square at the root, with empty quadrants below it. Insert a switch before depth 1 in chains of depths 2 and 3, or before depth 1 or 3 in a depth-5 chain. Exercise both branches with an empty arm and with a short arm. Disconnect the depth-5 chain for a separate control. Replace the switch with a zero- or one-count iterator at depths 1 and 3. Use gain 1, roughness .375, .6, 1 or 1.25, at 16². For unit roughness the root reads 1/3, 1/4 and 1/6 at depths 2, 3 and 5 even with the deep arm inactive. Disconnecting that arm gives 1. Across 68 settings **17,408/17,408** raw F32 pixels match, maximum error zero. Before the fix 8,192 matched and the maximum error was .355624951.

The renderer also checks the computed octave weights when culling tiny stamps. An original square 1/256 of the image width and height exercised gains .5, 1.5, 2, 3.25, −.75 and 1.875, with repeat counts 19, 211, 12003, 3, 1 and 5 respectively. The first three are centered. The next two add frame offset (1/64,1/32), and the last adds (−1/128,−1/64). Use seed `458527 + 31j + width` with one-based series index `j`. Compare 16², 32 × 16, 16 × 32, 64 × 32 and 32 × 64 in U16 and F32, with U8 and F16 at 16² and 64 × 32. Including the separate 16² F32 gain-1.5 single-stamp control, **92,416/92,416** pixels match in 85 renders, maximum error zero. The release regression also draws a visible background before 1,048,580 missed stamps at gain 2. The earlier renderer exhausted its visit budget.

The root table counts one original per distinct setting and excludes cook errors. The first version includes the depth and culling fixes. The second version records the complete depth-only comparison. The four 64² precision controls and the changed 32² F32 control were also repeated with culling active in v2 and kept the same counts. ### Projected weights and tap order in short directional blurs

The short oblique blur measures its reach using the stored horizontal and vertical direction components. It derives the first and last tap from the dominant component in texture coordinates. ### Stored levels when resizing a grayscale bitmap resource

The Bitmap node now filters power-of-two normalized grayscale resources at each factor-of-two step. It clamps at the resource edge and stores each intermediate level at the node's destination format. Bitmap and graph-input paths use the same level sampler. The previous Bitmap cook averaged the entire footprint in one pass for integer-ratio reductions and sampled the original image directly for enlargements.

The 3D fractal Voronoi graph requests its lookup at 1024 × 1. Its original procedural input has 1024 columns and 16 rows. For U16, take successive vertical pairs, compute (a+b+1) div 2, and repeat until one row remains. On the shuffled table, 70/1,024 stored texels previously matched, maximum two levels. On the affine table, 95/1,024 matched, also within two levels. The earlier graph-output tests masked the affine-table differences.

Use the [two procedural tables](#package-ownership-of-saved-function-calls), a second row shuffle using seed 1299709, and tables filled with zero or 32768. From the first shuffled table, also replace zeros with 64, clamp the maximum to 65471, take the 65535 complement, and replace each of the 16 rows in turn with the matching affine row. All 24 directly captured Bitmap outputs now match **24,576/24,576** U16 texels, maximum zero. For an independent check, generate a 1024 × 1 PNG from the repeated pair calculation and bind it in both applications. The preceding evaluator then reproduces every final pixel across the seven shuffled and three affine settings of each fractal Voronoi root, **7,168/7,168 per root**, maximum zero.

For a two-column regression use four rows. Fill the columns with 0 and 1000 respectively and add one at the bottom of each column. Resizing to 2 × 1 U16 stores 1 and 1001. The previous evaluator stored 0 and 1000.

For an independent Bitmap graph, generate U16 levels (573x+149y+97xy+317) mod 65536 at 64 × 32 and 32 × 64, and U8 levels (83x+151y+11xy+29) mod 256 at 64 × 32. A fourth 64 × 32 U16 image uses 514 floor(x/8), plus one where x mod 4 and y mod 4 are both 3. Use the 128 × 128 third generator from the [single-texel comparison](#one-differing-generator-texel-in-the-basic-spots-root). | Seed and disorder | Exact / total across nine renders | Maximum error | Varying reference coordinates |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 0, default | 144,288/147,456 | 2.98023224e-08 | 524 |
| 42, default | 144,385/147,456 | 2.98023224e-08 | 469 |
| 0, .35 | 144,726/147,456 | 2.98023224e-08 | 447 |

To test the addition order, capture the position in traversal order and the F32 contribution of every MaterialCraft stamp that covers each pixel. The seven quadrant subdivisions yield 16,384 leaves. Group the leaves by their first two quadrant choices, numbering each group from 0 to 15 in traversal order. Keep the 1,024 leaves inside each group in order. For each pixel, enumerate the orderings of the groups that touch it, and accumulate the original contributions one at a time in F32 starting from zero. Keep the orderings that produce the observed F32 bits. Find a single order of all 16 groups that satisfies these constraints across the image.

One group order per capture reproduces **442,368/442,368** pixels over all 27 renders, maximum zero. For example, the first default capture fits group order `0 12 9 1 4 5 13 10 14 15 8 11 6 7 2 3`. Fitting on part of each image also predicts withheld pixels. Exclude every coordinate with `(x + 3*y) % 5 == 0` and the coordinate (99,47) before choosing each order. An ascending search for the first compatible group order predicts **88,476/88,479** withheld pixels, maximum 1.49011612e−8. All nine default captures predict the held-out (99,47) value .15169809758663177.

In the default graph the four MaterialCraft contributions at (99,47), in its traversal order, are .05887965112924576, .031324971467256546, .02835862897336483 and .03313484787940979. Their accumulation order accounts for the U16 boundary at that coordinate. The observed changes between captures prevent a single fixed image from matching every repeat. These reordered images explain the disagreement. The original renderer counts above and the [125-setting root comparison](#gaussian-generators-and-spots-through-1024-pixels-per-side) remain the parity measurements.

### Grayscale conversion on the first bitmap filter pass

A normalized RGBA bitmap with grayscale output filters RGB at source precision on the first resize pass. An inherited top-level pixel ratio evaluates to 1 (square pixels). An absolute ratio of 0 stretches the pixels to the graph dimensions. ### Adding selected components of a vector quotient

A pixel function can select two components of a vector quotient, then add them. If both components feed only that sum, the numerator and reciprocal of the left component participate in one fused multiply-add with the rounded right component. An independent reader of the left component makes that lane round first and allows the right component to contract. Independent readers of both require both rounded values. Returning the quotient from a local function preserves these rules in the tested calls.

Divide normalized pixel-center coordinates by (3.625, −.71875). Select x and y, add in both orders, expose x, y or both beside the sum, and repeat x as both operands. At (0.15625,0.03125), x + y stores F32 word `b9c482a0` and y + x stores `b9c48280`. Repeat at 16² and 64 × 32, seeds 632137 + variant index and 633107 + variant index. The 12 renders match **13,824/13,824** pixels, maximum zero.

For an independent RGBA input use seeds S = 635791, 636119 and 636889 at 16², 32 × 64 and 64 × 32. Red is (((31x + 13y + 7xy + S) mod 353) − 151)/29. Green is (((13x + 59y + 17xy + S) mod 379) − 209)/37. Blue is (((73x + 31y + 5xy + S) mod 251) + 11)/61. Alpha is −(((37x + 23y + 13xy + S) mod 311) + 5)/73. Divide (red, green) by (blue, alpha) and repeat with the literal divisor. Exercise both addition orders, both single-lane readers, both lanes shared, x used twice, a call returning the quotient, and the call with x shared. Render all three shapes in F32 and add U8, U16 and F16 at 32 × 64.

### Pixel subtraction and texture coordinates at the panorama equator

At the equator, the panorama projection can produce an undefined horizontal texture coordinate alongside a finite vertical coordinate. Addressing the two axes independently fixes the sampled row. In the preceding projection stage, subtracting a selected product or quotient also preserves the operand sign when a component is used in a fused multiply-add.

Use the [five original color and mask fields](#adding-selected-components-of-a-vector-quotient), including the four-format 64² setting with source position (.984375,.5), patch position (.015625,.84375), patch turn .03515625 and source offset −.03515625. The source direction there is approximately (.99518466,−.09801697,−0.0). The reciprocal of its last component is negative infinity. The sampled coordinates include an F32 NaN with word `7fffffff` and vertical coordinate .5. Bilinear repeat samples both sides of the horizontal seam at that row. Rendering the complete image on the earlier build differed at 90 U8 pixels (maximum 119 levels) and 102 pixels each in U16, F16 and F32 (maxima 30,519 levels, .465576172 and .465690076).

Repeat the F32 setting while changing one control at a time. Set source latitude to .5 ± 1/8192, .46875 or .53125, or longitude to .5 or 0. Set either turn or both to zero. Vary the source offset by ±1/8192. Try alpha mode 0, the frame helper on, the effect disabled, the published defaults, a centered patch, and hardness 1. In the two settings immediately above and below the equator the earlier build already matched every pixel.

To isolate the arithmetic, record the rotated direction, raw center, reciprocal, scaled center, their two-component difference, projected coordinates, sampled patch, weight and final output at the three band settings and eight changed or default F32 settings. Subtracting two rounded vectors reproduced 24,232/37,120 difference vectors. Multiplying each raw center component by the reciprocal with the negated rotated component as the fused addend reproduced 37,120/37,120. After the change all nine diagnostics match in every selected component, including signed zero, infinities and NaN words, **334,080/334,080** pixels across 99 renders.

Multiply or divide pixel-center position by (3.6123411655426025,−.718791127204895), subtract the x and y components in both orders, expose x, y or both beside x − y, and repeat x − x. Use 16² and 64 × 32, seed 641933 + 83j + width, numbering the six product variants first, then the six quotient variants. At position (.15625,.03125), x − y in the product graph stores `3f163e75` and y − x stores `bf163e76`. For the signed field use the [independent quotient input formula and graph variants](#adding-selected-components-of-a-vector-quotient) at the same three sizes with seeds 656803, 657889 and 658451. Use subtraction in place of addition, retain the sampled divisors and repeat with literal divisors (−1.06719768,2.41659069).

For the texture read, divide floor(3p) − 1 by x − x at pixel-center coordinate p, producing negative infinity, NaN and positive infinity in successive thirds. Put this coordinate in x, y or both. On a finite axis use 1.5p − .12109375. Cross these layouts with nearest and bilinear in repeat and clamp. With seed S = 651913 + 109j at 16², 32 × 16 and 16 × 32, use an original RGBA field ((x+1)/64, (y+1)/64, ((3x+7y+S) mod 127)/128, 1−((x+2y+S) mod 8)/16). At 16² with invalid x and y = .67578125, nearest repeat reads red/green (.015625,.171875) and bilinear repeat reads (.1328125,.1767578125). In clamp the red value is .015625 for NaN and negative infinity and .25 for positive infinity.

For the second texture field, use the same coordinates and seed S = 657061 + 179j at 16 × 64, 64 × 16 and 32². Use RGBA components (((43x+67y+17xy+S) mod 271)−23)/274, (((17x+31y+7xy+S) mod 211)−15)/261, the indicator of (3x+11y+S) mod 11 = 7, and ((23x+137y+3xy+S) mod 251)/250. For variants k from 0 to 11 cycle x, y and both invalid, cycle nearest repeat, bilinear clamp, bilinear repeat and nearest clamp, and change input storage in groups of four from U8 to U16 to F16. Both roots contain two Distance nodes. Pixel ratio 0 scales each texel displacement by min(W,H)/axis length. Pixel ratio 1 uses texel distances directly. A source texel at index i has a stored coordinate given by the nearest even integer to (i + .5)65535/N on an axis of length N. Decode that word before subtracting the pixel center. A wrapped axis uses the image midpoint as its origin during subtraction. At 512 × 32, a site at (1,30) and strength 87.625 gives F32 word `3f68a0de` one texel to the right with horizontal wrapping and `3f68a0d2` with that axis open. Vertical wrapping alone leaves the latter word intact.

The propagation step covers the same fraction of each axis. For a step of j texels on the longest side L, point sampling on an axis of length N addresses offsets floor(.5 − jN/L) and floor(.5 + jN/L). Equal-distance candidates retain the current site. Among new candidates the observed priority is right, left, down, up, lower right, upper left, upper right and lower left. Rows increase downwards. With both axes open the final one-texel refinement remains in use.

For a small Euclidean example, tile a 32 × 16 mask with sites (9,13), (21,5) and (7,1). Give them source values .125, .25 and .375 with .0625 elsewhere, set strength 256, choose ratio 1 and disable Combine. The value at (31,10) is .125. For a tie test at 32² set the mask where x and y are both multiples of three or (x + 2y) mod 7 equals 3. Give each source texel value (1 + x + 32y)/1024. At strength 256 the Manhattan result at (30,8) selects (29,8). With Chebyshev distance, (14,0) selects (15,0) and (19,0) selects (18,0).

For the dense-mask series use the size, metric and tiling combinations (32², Euclidean, both), (64 × 16, Euclidean, both), (16 × 32, Euclidean, both), (32², Euclidean, neither), (32², Manhattan, both), (32², Chebyshev, both), (64 × 32, Euclidean, horizontal) and (32 × 64, Euclidean, vertical). Number them g = 0–7. For setting t = 0–5 use seed S = 711709 + 19g + 109t and strength 256, 206.5, 95.75, 256, 133.25 or 78.5 respectively. Set the mask where (17x + 31y + 5xy + S) mod 251 is below 64, 107, 144 or 193 at t = 0, 1, 2 or 5. At t = 3 use the lattice from the tie test. At t = 4 require x mod 2 = y mod 2 and (x + y) mod 3 different from zero. Use source (1 + x + Wy)/(WH) with Combine disabled.

### Diagonal mip selection on rotated rectangular bitmaps

The first different stage of Radial Blur Grayscale was the automatic bitmap filter in its first pattern graph. A 32 × 64 modular-and-impulse input at default parameters gave 345/2,048 exact U16 pattern pixels, maximum 405 levels. The downstream blend gave 527/2,048, maximum 138 U16 levels. At the F32 output 527/2,048 matched, maximum .00210574269. The input and all three transformed fields already matched.

Retain the graph’s original sample count and per-stamp opacity, limiting only the number of visits. With 64 samples, .125 turns and the center offset (0,0), the first 41 draws matched 2,048/2,048 pixels. Including the 42nd draw, rotated by 41/512 turns, matched 338/2,048 with maximum 404 U16 levels. With the new filter both prefixes and the complete draw match. A separate one-stamp graph reproduces the transition at either orientation of a 2:1 rectangle. At ±41/512 turns the reference automatic filter selects the same level as bilinear sampling. At 42/512 it selects a coarser level.

For a 64 × 32 original byte image use ((17x+59y+9xy+7) mod 251) + 4[(x+3y) mod 7 < 3]. Use one full-size, centered grayscale bitmap stamp, tiling off, opacity one, and read F32 at (32,16). At rotations 40/512, 41/512, 42/512 and −41/512 the stored bits are `3f1aeb9b`, `3f1c699c`, `3f0eca8f` and `3effd300`. For the wider sweep use 32 × 64, 64 × 32, 64² and 32 × 128. At the first size use the matching byte output of the first transform in the modular-and-impulse graph. At the three other sizes replace 7 in the byte field with 7j, with j = 1, 2, 3. At all four sizes render turns (39,40,41,42,43)/512, 41/512 ± 2⁻¹⁵, 41/512 ± 2⁻¹², −41/512, 0, .125 and .25−41/512. Automatic and bilinear each match **159,744/159,744** F32 pixels across 52 settings.

The [two-by-two pixel group](#automatic-bitmap-stamp-levels-at-neighboring-pixels) supplies the two screen derivatives in texels. Truncate each signed component to nine fraction bits. For each texture coordinate, align the two screen derivatives with one extra fraction bit at the larger exponent before taking their sum and difference. Evaluate both diagonals. Weight the larger magnitude by 11/16, add a quarter of its input unit and truncate to nine fraction bits at the resulting exponent. For the smaller magnitude with nine-bit integer significand m (including its implicit leading bit, scaled by 512), use floor((121m+32)/512) times its input unit. The maximum of both axial and both diagonal footprints selects the level at the existing half-level thresholds.

Generate a mip chain with a constant value equal to its level number and read the selected level using explicit gradients. The three fixed regression matrices, written in texels divided by 2048, are ((1864,−2248),(1874,861)), ((1884,649),(1884,649)) and ((1814,−841),(−2192,−1450)). Their measured levels are 1, 0 and 0, respectively. In the independent dense series draw four F32 components uniformly from −1 to 1 with random seed 763451. Use 131,072 matrices in order. For the first 32,768 make the two screen derivatives equal, and for the next 32,768 make them opposites. For the following 16,384 set both second components to zero. For the next 16,384 set the second screen derivative to zero. Scale each matrix by 2ᵉ × 1.4140625 × u divided by its approximate unquantized footprint, with e a uniform integer from 0 through 6 and u uniform from .997 to 1.003. The unquantized footprint uses max + 11/32 min for each axis and 11/16 of that norm for both diagonals.

### Parameter-controlled sizes and half-precision pattern backgrounds

A normalized integer background can cross a half-precision storage boundary before the first pattern draws, even when its dimensions already match the output. In the measured cases this happens when exactly one of the upstream image and the F16 pattern output uses a size controlled by an exposed parameter. Computing a size solely from the current image dimensions follows the fixed-size path. The same distinction applies to normalized Blend inputs.

For a minimal grayscale control, connect a U8 input holding 58/255 to the background of a 16² F16 pattern. Draw one centered, full-size square in additive mode with gray tint 3/32768, alpha 1 and unit overall opacity. Give the source and the pattern relative size offsets of (0,0). In a size function, read an exposed float set to .375, then return the original (0,0). With the function on just one side the stored output is **.2274169921875**. With fixed sizes on both sides, only a read of `$size` or `$sizelog2`, or an exposed size function on both sides, it is **.2275390625**. The difference is the initial conversion of the normalized background toward zero at half precision. Supplying the same field as a nearest-filtered bitmap stamp retains its original sampling precision.

For the gray and RGBA controls, run matching U8 and U16 input bridges, then repeat with F16 and F32 sources. The single-square gray tint is 3/32768 and the RGBA tint is (.4814453125,.187835693359375,.5118408203125,.734375). In color use (.22745098,.49411765,.52931082,.61328125) for the constant input. At size index j = 0, 1, 2, 3, use 16², 32 × 16, 16 × 32 and 32², with seed 843173 + 19j. For j > 0 use (((73+4c)x + 29y + 13xy + 37j + 47c) mod 997)/996, where c is the zero-based channel. The j = 3 source is 16 × 32. At the constant setting compare all four output formats. Add F16 and F32 for j = 1, then F16 for j = 2 and 3. Exercise source only, output only, both, neither, and the nearest-filtered bitmap slot with tint .71875.

In the separate 64² fading-square test use variation .2, tint 1, and the original 128² input reduced to a U8 background. Repeat on the field ((47x+83y+11xy+5) mod 257)/256, including tint .34375. Change the requested relative size using an exposed integer pair, a converted float, a Boolean choice, or a read followed by a constant result. Include a Boolean whose two branches both return (0,0), and a size-only choice between (0,0) and (1,0) based on the aspect ratio. An exposed setting that genuinely enlarged the result also matched. ### Pattern draw order for fixed and runtime image slots

Overlapping bitmap stamps with constant image selectors draw in the order each image slot is first used. When any visited bitmap quadrant reads a changing image selector, the slots draw in ascending input-port order. This applies to both grayscale and RGBA. The selector can return the same integer in both cases. A visited image with zero size, zero tint or an off-canvas footprint still establishes the order. A disconnected quadrant, an empty pattern, a procedural shape and an unbound getter retained first-use order in the controls.

Use a black background and three overlapping bitmap quadrants that select slots (1,0,1). At successive depths use sizes (1,1), (2,2) and (4,4), nearest filtering, overall opacity 1 and a constant image per slot. In grayscale use byte levels 128 and 255. ### Unbound integer variables in node properties

An integer getter in a node property reads zero for an unbound reserved name. A definedness test on that name returns false. In the same property, the tiling flags and pixel ratio return 3 and 1 with default tiling. The distinction affects a Blend even when the property reads the seed and then returns a fixed opacity or mode.

Use a Uniform node at 8 × 4 with F32 RGBA output and seeds 0, 31 and 12071. ### Uniform channel width and grayscale rounding in node properties

Grayscale Uniform preserves a scalar input directly. A fixed four-component color sums red, green and blue in that order, then divides by three. A runtime four-component color multiplies each of those channels by F32(1/3) first, then adds the three rounded contributions from left to right. Alpha does not enter the mean. A three-component function result yields zero in grayscale and opaque black in RGBA. Packing the same RGB with an explicit alpha restores its color. Graph inspection keeps the original RGB parameter available.

Use (1,2⁻²³,−1,.59375) to distinguish the two means. The fixed F32 result has bits `332aaaab` and the exposed result has bits `33000000`. A fixed signed tuple (−65536,65536,2⁻⁹,.5) yields `3a2aaaab`. Feed the scalar with bits `3ed51632` to either channel mode. In grayscale, it retains that word. The controls also cover three primaries, equal-channel levels, signed colors and permutations of nearly canceling channels.

For the first dependency series, compare a literal, a folded sum with zero, a bound RGBA color, the same color plus a zero vector, and a sequence that reads the bound color before returning the literal. Also read image size before the literal, take alpha from the bound input, select between the bound and fixed colors, return a scalar channel, or return a scalar after reading size. Use the signed tuple above, (1.75,−.875,−.25,.5), (.1,.1,.1,.25), three copies of `3ed51632` with alpha .875, the HDR cancellation tuple, and (−.4,1.875,.1375,−.5). ### Directional blur weights at signed and large rotations

A directional blur accepts signed angles outside its slider range. A parameter check previously clipped every angle beyond ±33 turns to the endpoint. The regression uses a unit impulse in each of two rectangular images and reads the center pixel and its immediate neighbor along the longer axis. At strength 4, the F32 turn word `c5f564d9` on a 64 × 16 image gives center `3f0f4d94` and neighbor `3e6164db`. The turn word `46f0483d` on a 16 × 64 image gives `3f17a518` and `3e50b5d1`. Authored rotations can reach both results through the ordinary parameter resolver.

For shorter phases, convert the turns to F32 radians. Use the magnitude of the radians for sine and add F32(π/2) to that magnitude for cosine. Subtract the nearest number of half turns using three parts of π. Start with 3.140625, round the remainder of π to F32 for the middle part, then round the residual to F32 for the low part. A fused multiply and subtraction produces each successive remainder. Restore the sign of the sine after odd half turns. Feeding those remainders to the existing sine polynomial predicts all 64 independently selected axes where the previous and revised reductions disagree. Both predictions fit the 16 controls. All 128 near-axis measurements admit the revised coefficient, up from 125. The earlier [equal-remainder pair](#equal-reduced-phases-with-distinct-rectangular-blur-coefficients) illustrates the lost bit.

At large phases the implementation evaluates the sine in double precision and stores the F32 result. Eight deliberately distinguishable axes just below 10,000 radians select the split reduction. Eight just above select the wide sine. Across the three large-angle and transition series, the wide sine falls within the observed interval on 170/171 selected axes at or above 10,000 radians. The remaining case at 10011.0888671875 radians differs by one F32 word. Finite turns whose conversion to F32 radians overflows produce a cook error.

### Shared random draws in pattern branches and returned color channels

In a pattern tint, a random draw used by a conditional arm and a later channel keeps its place in the order of the arms. The condition runs first. With the false arm selected, the tested draws shared with the skipped true arm run before the false result. With the true arm selected, its result runs before draws needed from the false arm. A scalar selection from a packed vector visits the supplying component. In a straight-line called function with scalar inputs, the first uses of those inputs determine their evaluation order. Repeated reads reuse the same draw.

Use one full-coverage rectangle, additive color on a black background, with unit alpha and independent unit draws A, B, C, D and E. Set the RGB result to (if take then lerp(A,B,C) else D, E, A). At seed 31 the F32 words for true are `3f51c505 3e9a198c 3f3457e6` and for false are `3f5a33c2 3f46fab2 3f3457e6`. Replace the false arm with lerp(C,B,D) and return D in blue. True gives `3f51c505 3f5b5a9e 3e9a198c` and false gives `3f3cc6a3 3e9a198c 3f46fab2`. Test all four combinations of two Boolean inputs when nesting the arms. Use 16², 32 × 16 and 16 × 32 with seeds 31, 12071 and 68047 respectively, and range inputs .25, .625 and .9375.

Compare the whole result and a single selected result assembled with the caller's next draw. Repeat with three return channels derived from one packed RGBA argument. The four F32 settings use 16² seed 31 with the switch off and on, 32 × 16 seed 12071 with it off, and 16 × 32 seed 68047 with it on. ### Returned channels of a packed argument in pattern functions

A pattern call that returns channels selected from a packed argument draws the caller’s scalar sources in the order the result needs them. Selecting the same source twice reuses its draw. The evaluator traces an argument through a function containing only typed argument reads, vector packs and channel selections. A scalar selection can then evaluate the supplying register directly. A whole vector result evaluates the supplying registers in return order. Both four-float and color-widget defaults represent a four-channel argument.

Use the [full-coverage rectangle and seed-31 draw sequence](#shared-random-draws-in-pattern-branches-and-returned-color-channels). Pack four independent unit draws A, B, C and D into RGBA and pass them as one argument. Return (D,C,A), (A,D,B), (B,B,B) or (D,D,C). At seed 31 the whole (D,C,A) return has RGB words `3f3457e6 3f5a33c2 3f46fab2`. Return (D, first channel of the call, next draw E) instead to get `3f3457e6 3f3457e6 3f5a33c2`. Repeat with the caller selecting the third or second returned channel and with a Boolean selecting between D and the call’s first channel. ### Finite loops that reach a fixed point in path-length graphs

A finite function loop can reach a state that repeats on every remaining iteration. At a pair of consecutive condition checks the evaluator compares the random stream, the written variable names, the values visible inside the function and the assignments visible to its caller. Identical state gives the same subsequent body and condition. The evaluator returns the last body result. It samples these pairs at powers of two to avoid copying state on every iteration of a changing loop. Float comparisons preserve the component bits, including the sign of zero.

For a small reproduction of [the path-length cases](#skipped-loops-and-path-buffers), start with a zero RGBA F32 image. At (0,0) store (1,1/W,1/H,1/W) and at (1,0) store (N+1,1,1,1/W), where W and H are the input dimensions. On row 1 use the first N positions of (.21875,.34375), (.75,.390625), (.640625,.796875), (.390625,.84375), (.125,.546875), then duplicate the first position. Set blue to 1 and alpha to −.25 for the first point, −.125 for the duplicate and −1 for interior points. Use (W,H,N) of (4,4,1), (4,4,2), (8,8,3) and (16,16,5). Set scale to (1.25,.8125). Test no passthrough with intermediate lengths off and on at F32, passthrough with intermediate lengths on at F32, then intermediate lengths on with passthrough off at U16, F16 and U8. The seed is 128101 + 11N + the zero-based setting index.

In the 8² three-vertex test, the reference header at (1,0) stores 3.816796064376831. Starting at iteration 1, the observed cursor and sampled position are both (0,0). The length, sampled texel and exported assignments are identical on consecutive visits. MaterialCraft gives the same F32 word at this pixel with an experimental cap of 1, 2, 3, 4, 8, 16, 32 or 64. The authored loop allows 65,536 iterations. A selected-pixel trace also found continuing sums in the resized-input cases below.

### Sampling both passes of a long oblique blur

The [periodic RGB impulse](#isolated-sample-coordinates-in-the-two-hq-blur-roots) isolates the transverse sample positions on each pass. Keep the angle and dimensions fixed and change only the radius. For a 128 × 256 image at .337890625 turns, moving from radius 6.71875 to 7.375 changes the forward interpolation weight by one unit of 1/256 texel at 344 of 12,800 common sampled positions. The inverse changes at 264 of 11,776. The slope uses the ratio of the two already rounded projected extents. For the two horizontal passes, let u and v be texel-center coordinates and s the signed UV slope on that pass. The forward pass forms the fused product (−s)(1−u) + v, then adds s/2. The inverse pass first rounds s × u, then adds v and subtracts s/2. Both vertical passes form the fused s × v + u before subtracting s/2. These orderings agree with all 820,992 recovered interpolation weights in 29 angle, size and radius combinations.

Five [resized path-length settings](#finite-loops-that-reach-a-fixed-point-in-path-length-graphs) previously exhausted the execution budget. At output (1,0), seven initial increments lead into a period of four. The four measured F32 increments are .23174433410167694, 2.1718389987945557, .9635875225067139 and 1.26210618019104. ### Three terminal children in seven-level quadrant trees

Dirt 3 draws 12,288 additive leaves at depth seven. Each depth-six quadrant has children in slots 0, 1 and 3. The previous renderer ordered the complete four-child case and visited the three-child case in sequence. On a white F32 background, repeat the [seven-level square experiment](#compositing-complete-seven-level-additive-quadrant-trees), disconnecting slot 2 from every depth-six quadrant. Separately omitting each of slots 0, 1, 2 and 3 produced the same ordering in all 92,160 overlapping samples per omission. An unconnected routing dot on the complete four-child graph also retained that order. Across its 120 renders MaterialCraft improved from 1,891,328/1,966,080 to **1,966,080/1,966,080**, maximum error zero.

An independent comparison labelled all 64 subtrees reached after the third subdivision. Pair them in 63 round-robin rounds with the same white background, −1 and 2⁻²⁵ square opacities and zero roughness. Translate each pair into one of 32 upper-half tiles of the 8 × 8 grid. Across all 2,016 comparisons the four consecutive subtrees of each grandchild stayed together. The sixteen groups of 768 leaves followed the order measured in the four-child case. MaterialCraft uses the connected terminal child count to find group boundaries before dropping stamps that miss the sample grid. It checks the node kinds that the renderer actually visits.

### Parent and leaf draws in Fur 2 and Gaussian Spots 2

Fur 2 and Gaussian Spots 2 each draw 4,096 procedural stamps at depth six and four children per stamp at depth seven. The group boundary must precede the parent draw, including when its geometry misses the sample grid. MaterialCraft now records the boundary on entry to each of the sixteen grandchildren and preserves the original order of draws inside it. The renderer recognizes regular additive grayscale trees with the measured depth and child counts.

### Untiled draw order for two and four children below depth seven

Start with the [original paired-square controls](#tile-copies-and-the-draw-order-in-clouds-2). Each of the 64 depth-three subtrees has 256 depth-seven parents in Morton order. With two children per parent, the order can change after parent 28 inside a subtree. With four children it can change after parents 68 and 136. To resolve the four-child order, repeat the 63 pairing rounds on a white 256² F32 image. Offset the second member’s parent frame by (−1,+1)/128 and (0,−1)/128 in separate runs. Compare the paired parent positions inside each 16 × 16 readout, keeping destination coordinates 2 through 13 on both axes. The three parent intervals give 18,144 relative orders between distinct subtrees. The renderer records the corresponding contiguous stretches of parent visits before empty pixel coverage is discarded. It uses their measured order for active, untiled, additive grayscale quadrant trees of this shape.

Use the [original paired-square tree](#untiled-draw-order-for-two-and-four-children-below-depth-seven), with 64 subtrees, 256 depth-seven parents per subtree and two depth-eight children per parent. The marker pixels are consistent with a change in parent order at indices 211, 144 and 212 respectively within a divided subtree. Each graph has two parent ranges. Displacing the competing interior squares by opposing one-cell offsets distinguished 8,064 cross-subtree relations per graph. One sequence of 29 contiguous draw ranges fits all three graphs when the splits are expressed in physical tile copies. In this sequence, splits occur every 5,460 copies drawn in composite order. The first three divided prefixes may finish in either of the last two subtrees before their continuations end. Later cuts can change the order of entire subtrees. MaterialCraft checks those boundaries before using either measured sequence.

Six separately constructed graphs varied which parents put children on the seam. Use every 32nd parent, every 64th, every 16th in even subtrees, every 32nd shifted by three times the subtree index, every 16th except every 64th in subtrees 16–23, or every 16th in the first two of every four subtrees and every 32nd in the other two. ### Two-child draw order when neighboring subtrees cross different tile batches

In the two-child additive square tree, groups of 256 depth-seven parents each contribute 768 logical stamps. Boundary crossings increase the number of physical draws in each group. Three leading batches begin at groups 24, 40 and 8. Three other batches first consume two subtrees from groups 50, 54 or 58 and then continue from groups 16, 32 or 0, respectively. Each batch ends after 5,460 tile copies. The continuation order depends on which of the three paired batches reaches the split one subtree early. MaterialCraft selects the observed 26–29 draw runs from those physical counts. A split can separate two copies of the same stamp.

Repeat the [two-child square controls](#wrapped-draw-order-for-two-children-below-depth-seven). In each of 64 subtrees, count parent positions p from 0 to 255 in quadrant traversal order. Move the two terminal slots of selected parents to the horizontal tile edge and keep the others in the interior. For the first six distributions select every 32nd parent, every 64th, every 16th in even groups only, every 32nd with phase 3g, every 16th except every 64th in groups 16–23, and every 16th in groups divisible by four with every 32nd elsewhere. Here g is the zero-based subtree index. For a second series, give groups 0–7, 16–23 and 32–39 independently a period of 16 or 64. Keep period 32 elsewhere and select (p + 3g) modulo the period equal to zero. These eight patterns exercise every combination of split positions.

Compare each pair of the 64 subtrees at all 256 parent positions by adding −1 and 2⁻²⁵ in opposite orders against a unit background. Displaced readouts distinguish segments that otherwise never overlap. All 4,128,768 pair decisions in the eight-pattern series agreed with the resulting draw order. Six other distributions matched 3,096,576/3,096,576 decisions. Five independently authored distributions with the same per-subtree copy totals as individual cloud renders matched 2,580,480/2,580,480. To reproduce the five totals, use the exposed 128² generator at seeds 42 and 43, 128 × 256 at seed 139711, 32 × 64 at seed 175302 and 512 × 128 at seed 175883. For each group distribute half the extra copies in evenly spaced pairs and place an odd remaining copy in the first parent. Eight full F32 frames from each of the eight patterns and five matched distributions gave 6,815,744/6,815,744 pixels, maximum zero.

## 2026-11-20 root comparisons

### Hue, saturation, lightness and Replace Color

The HSL primitive adds twice each slider's displacement from .5 to saturation and lightness, then clamps. For an HDR input it divides RGB by the largest of 1 and the three input channels before adjusting color and restores that gain afterwards. With default settings pure red produces (.999877930, .0001220703125, .00109827518) in the reference. Equal-channel .125 gray with saturation .75 produces (.1875,.0625,.0625). Changing lightness to .75 instead gives (.625,.625,.625).

### Signed Sharpen stencils and stored inputs

Sharpen preserves negative lobes in floating-point output and uses the input's working storage when resizing. Its four-neighbor stencil starts with the weighted left texel. It adds the center, right, top and bottom terms in that order, fusing the product and addition at each step. With horizontal weight H and vertical weight V, the center weight is 1+2(H+V). H and V scale intensity by the shorter output side divided by the respective axis length. The two earlier sign and resizing regressions and two further accumulation checks failed on the preceding implementations. All 256 release node tests, formatting, strict workspace Clippy, dependency layers and WebAssembly passed.

| Original probe | Renders | Exact / compared | Maximum error |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| Impulse, signed ramp and constant, U16 and F32 sources | 16 | 5,632/5,632 | 0 in all four output formats |
| Grayscale and RGBA with output size inherited from the input | 108 | 10,512/10,512 | 0 in all four output formats |
| Output size set by parent | 108 | 38,549/38,832 comparable | 0 / 0 / 0 / 1.87000686 in U8 / U16 / F16 / F32 |
| Independent signed field with five nonzero strengths and changed sizes | 80 | 16,417/16,704 | 4.39762998 F32 |
| Dirt 4 and its second version, shared 2² sources | 8 | 136/136 | 0 F32 |

For the impulse matrix, place a single white texel at (8,8) in a black 16² image. Render at intensity one in all four formats and at 32² F32. At 16² the floating-point output is 5 at the center, −1 at its four axial neighbors and zero at the diagonals. In U8 and U16 the center is white and the neighbors black. Add the 16² signed field (((x+3y) mod 17)−5)/8 at intensities .375 and 0, and a flat .28125 at intensity 1. Use F32 inputs or clip and round to U16, and seeds 138559+11j in the order F32, F16, U8, U16, enlarged F32, two ramps and flat.

For the input-size and parent-size matrices, use source extents 2², 8×4 and 16². Test grayscale and four-channel inputs in U16 and F32. In channel c use level Q=(7919x+21473y+1103xy+2927c+139m+58997) mod 65536 for m=0 or 2. For m=1 use 59841−223c where (x+y+c) mod 3=0, and 3431+125c elsewhere. Write Q for U16 or Q/19001−.8125 for F32. Use the following cases with seed 134381+19j+i, where i is 1 for U16 and 3 for F32. The parent-size matrix has four additional size discrepancies at a requested 1². The reference returned 8×4. The pixel totals exclude those four outputs.

| Requested extent relative to source | Strength | Field m | Stored output |

For the independent field use Q=(269x+1723y+257xy+9587c+7919((x+3y+5c) mod 13)+7537) mod 65536 at 8×4 or 16². Write Q for U16 or (Q−31007)/15019+.03125(x mod 3) for F32. Use F32 output. At the source extent use strengths 0, 1, .375, .8125, 1.34375 and 2.71875, then double both axes at 0 and .8125, and halve both axes at 0 and 1.34375. Use seed 142867+19j. ### Sharpen at reduced output sizes

When the source is up to twice the output size on either axis and at least as large on both, Sharpen reads the center and four neighbors from the stored source. Neighbor offsets span one source texel. The stencil weights still use the output aspect ratio. A unit-strength white impulse at (8,8) in a black 16² F32 image isolates the spacing.
